summary: In July 1187 Saladin, the Ayyubid sultan of Egypt and Syria, destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin and went on to take Jerusalem and nearly every crusader town except Tyre. Pope Gregory VIII called a new crusade, and three of Europe's most powerful rulers took the cross: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England. Frederick marched overland, fought his way through Byzantine territory and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, but drowned in Anatolia in June 1190, and most of his army went home. Richard and Philip came by sea, conquering Cyprus on the way, and in July 1191 joined the two-year siege of Acre, which surrendered. Philip then went home. Richard beat Saladin at Arsuf and twice came close to Jerusalem but did not besiege it. The Treaty of Jaffa (September 1192) left Jerusalem in Muslim hands, restored a coastal crusader kingdom from Tyre to Jaffa and opened the holy places to Christian pilgrims.
casualties: No reliable total exists; the two-year siege of Acre alone is estimated to have cost tens of thousands of lives on both sides, many from disease, and about 2,700 Muslim prisoners were executed there in August 1191.

brief.hook: In 1187 Saladin crushed the crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem; three of Europe's mightiest kings took the cross to win it back.

sides.who: Armies of the Holy Roman Empire, England and its Angevin lands, and France, with the barons of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and the military orders
The Ayyubid sultanate of Egypt and Syria, with Turkish horse archers, Bedouin and Sudanese troops
The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia, which fought Barbarossa's German army in 1190

brief.resultLine: By the Treaty of Jaffa, on 2 September 1192, Richard and Saladin agreed a three-year truce: Jerusalem stayed Muslim, but unarmed Christian pilgrims could visit it.

strategies.name: The fighting march
strategies.text: Richard marched down the coast in tight order, infantry and crossbowmen shielding the knights, with the fleet alongside. He beat Saladin at Arsuf and regained the coast as far as Jaffa.

strategies.name: Guarding Jerusalem
strategies.text: Saladin had the walls of Ascalon pulled down and held on to Jerusalem. Richard twice came within reach but turned back, fearing that an army besieging it far from the sea would be trapped by a relief force.

impact: A coastal Kingdom of Jerusalem, from Tyre to Jaffa, survived for another century.
Richard's conquest of Cyprus gave the crusaders a lasting Christian base in the eastern Mediterranean.
Saladin died in 1193, and his heirs quarrelled and divided his empire.
Richard was captured in Austria on the way home and released only for a ransom of 150,000 marks.

details: Saladin's victory at Hattin on 4 July 1187 and his capture of Jerusalem that October left the crusaders holding little but Tyre. Pope Gregory VIII called a new crusade, and Frederick took the cross at the 'Court of Christ' in Mainz in March 1188. The first of the three monarchs to leave, he mustered his army at Regensburg in May 1189 and chose the overland route through Hungary, the Balkans and Anatolia.

Released by Saladin, King Guy found Conrad of Montferrat in control of Tyre and turned instead to the rich port of Acre. His small army, reinforced by fleets of crusaders from northern Europe and Italy, besieged the city, but Saladin's army in turn surrounded the besiegers. Both sides were supplied by sea, and the siege dragged on for nearly two years amid disease, hunger and repeated battles.

Emperor Isaac II Angelos distrusted Frederick, refused him the imperial title and held his envoys, while an Ayyubid ambassador was at his court. The crusaders broke with Byzantium, seized Philippopolis (Plovdiv) and its supplies on 26 August and occupied much of the surrounding country into November. Around 22 November they routed a Byzantine force under Manuel Kamytzes that had been sent to ambush their supply train, before eventually crossing into Asia.

Although promised safe passage by the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, the Germans faced constant Turkish hit-and-run attacks as they crossed Anatolia. Short of food and horses, Frederick decided to seize the Seljuk capital, Iconium (Konya), ruled by Kilij Arslan II. On 18 May 1190 the crusaders defeated the Turkish army there and sacked the city, gaining the supplies they needed to continue toward Armenian Cilicia.

While crossing the Saleph (Göksu) river in Cilicia, the elderly emperor was thrown from his horse and drowned. Much of his army returned to Germany by sea, partly because an imperial election was expected. His son Frederick of Swabia led the remaining few thousand men to Antioch, where fever thinned them further, and then to Acre, where he died in the winter of 1190–91.

Henry II of England and Philip II of France had made peace in January 1188 to go on crusade and raised the 'Saladin tithe', a tax on income and movable goods, to pay for it. Henry died in July 1189 and his son Richard took his place. The two kings left Vézelay together on 4 July 1190 and parted at Lyon, Richard heading for Marseille and Philip for Genoa, agreeing to meet in Sicily.

King Tancred of Sicily had imprisoned Richard's sister Joan, widow of the previous king. Richard seized Messina on 4 October 1190 and secured her release. The crusaders wintered in Sicily, where Richard and Philip fell out after Richard broke off his betrothal to Philip's half-sister Alys to marry Berengaria of Navarre. Philip sailed for the Holy Land on 30 March 1191; Richard followed on 10 April.

A storm scattered Richard's fleet, and ships carrying Joan, Berengaria and crusade treasure were driven to Cyprus, whose ruler Isaac Komnenos seized the treasure. Richard landed at Limassol on 6 May, married Berengaria there and, when Isaac turned hostile, conquered the whole island within weeks. Cyprus became a lasting Latin kingdom and a base for the crusader states; Richard later sold it to Guy of Lusignan.

Leopold V of Austria arrived with the remaining German forces in spring 1191 and Philip with the French in April. Richard reached Acre on 8 June and pressed the siege with new siege engines, and the garrison surrendered on 12 July. The victors quarrelled over the spoils: Richard threw down Leopold's banner, and the kings backed rival claimants, Guy and Conrad, for the crown of Jerusalem.

Frustrated with Richard and, in Philip's case, in poor health, the French king and Duke Leopold of Austria took their forces home in August 1191. Philip left behind 7,000 French crusaders and 5,000 silver marks to pay them, under the command of the duke of Burgundy. Richard was left as the sole royal leader of the crusade, with the dispute over the crown of Jerusalem settled for the moment: Guy would reign, and Conrad would succeed him.

Saladin tried to negotiate the release of the captured Acre garrison, which included women and children, but the talks dragged on. On 20 August Richard, judging that Saladin was stalling, had about 2,700 Muslim prisoners beheaded in full view of Saladin's army, which tried in vain to rescue them. Saladin responded by killing the Christian prisoners he held. The memory of the massacre embittered the rest of the war, and Muslim soldiers took revenge when they stormed Jaffa a year later.

Richard marched south along the coast toward Jaffa, the port he needed for any attack on Jerusalem, with his fleet alongside. Saladin harassed the column for days, then committed his army on the plain north of Arsuf. The crusaders kept their formation until the Hospitallers charged, and Richard turned it into a general counter-attack that routed the Ayyubid army. Saladin's army survived, but his reputation suffered and Richard took Jaffa.

Talks with Saladin's brother al-Adil, including a proposal that he marry Richard's sister Joan, came to nothing. In winter the crusaders advanced inland, spent Christmas at Latrun and reached Beit Nuba, about 12 miles from Jerusalem, after Saladin had been forced to dismiss much of his army. Cold, rain and hail, and the fear of being trapped by a relief army during a siege, led the leaders to retreat to the coast.

The nobles of the kingdom chose Conrad of Montferrat as king, and Richard had to accept it, compensating Guy with Cyprus. Before he could be crowned, Conrad was stabbed to death by two Assassins in the streets of Tyre. Eight days later Richard's nephew Henry of Champagne married the heiress Queen Isabella and became ruler. Many suspected that Richard had arranged the killing.

Through the winter Richard's men refortified Ascalon, which Saladin had demolished, and in spring negotiations and skirmishing continued. On 22 May the crusaders took the fortified town of Darum on the frontier of Egypt after five days of fierce fighting. Richard and most of his council saw Egypt as the base of Saladin's power and favoured attacking it rather than Jerusalem.

The army again marched inland and came within sight of Jerusalem in June 1192. The leaders were split: Richard and most of the council wanted to strike at Egypt, while the duke of Burgundy, leading the French, insisted on attacking Jerusalem directly. Neither faction was strong enough on its own, and the crusaders withdrew once more without laying siege to the city.

In July Saladin suddenly attacked and took Jaffa, though he lost control of soldiers still angry over the Acre massacre. Richard, about to leave for England, sailed down with a little over 2,000 men, stormed ashore and drove the Ayyubids out. When Saladin counter-attacked at dawn, Richard's crossbowmen inflicted heavy losses on his lightly armoured troops and the attack failed, strengthening the coastal crusader states.

Negotiated with the help of Balian of Ibelin, the truce left Jerusalem under Muslim rule but allowed unarmed Christian pilgrims and merchants to visit it, and guaranteed safe passage through Palestine for Christians and Muslims. The crusaders kept the coast from Tyre to Jaffa, while Ascalon, its walls demolished, went back to Saladin. Richard sailed for home on 9 October 1192, leaving Jerusalem in Muslim hands until a later crusade briefly regained it by treaty in 1229.
